c: God’s Covenant with Noah
The first explicit reference to a covenant in Scripture occurs immediately after the Flood (
The corruption and violence of the human race had provoked God’s anger (
), but his gracious favor remained with Noah (
). When God charged Noah to build an ark to escape the impending deluge (
), he also promised to establish a covenant with him (
). God took the initiative to bind himself again to human beings and to the whole creation despite human faithlessness (see

). Through this covenant, God guaranteed that he would maintain a relationship with this one family even as other divine-human relationships were being severed. God’s covenant promise to Noah came with his command to build an ark (
); Noah’s receipt of the covenant blessing depended on his obedience to this divine command (
When Noah made an offering to God after the Flood (
), God elaborated on his covenant with Noah, indicating that it was a universal covenant with humans and with all living creatures (
). God promised never to send such a flood again as judgment on the world.

This covenant helps us understand God as a covenant maker. Although human beings deserve punishment because of their wickedness, God withholds ultimate destruction. God’s covenant with Noah did not establish an intimate relationship between God and each living being, but it recalibrated moral and ecological life to be as God intended it (
), leaving open the possibility of a more intimate covenant to come (see

). Despite their evil, human beings are allowed to live in God’s world and seek a deeper relationship with the world’s Creator during their time on earth. God’s later covenants with his people made intimacy with him freely available to all (see

God’s first post-flood speech opens and closes with blessing (
). In it, human and animal relationships are again defined, with some modification of the original created order. The sanctity of life is given special focus.
Be fruitful and multiply:
The blessing and mandate first given to Adam (
) are now reissued to Noah, the “Adam” of the newly cleansed world in need of repopulation.
There are two modifications to the original created order. (1) Previously, humans reigned over
the animals
), but now animals would live in
terror
of humans (similar military language is found in
). (2) The animals’ terror was related to a change in human diet. Humans were now permitted to eat the meat of animals to supplement their subsistence on grains, fruits, and vegetables (
A key restriction is imposed. Since blood was identified with life, it had to be drained from a slain animal before its
meat
could be eaten (see
). The law of Moses prohibited eating animals that died naturally, since their blood had not been drained (
). God provided animal blood to atone for human sin (
Violence, including murder, was a major factor in bringing about God’s judgment of the flood (
). At this new beginning for humans, God affirmed the sanctity of human life and established a system of retributive justice for the taking of human life (see also
” Theme Note). The function of law is to restrain human wickedness and preserve moral order. This law was further developed in the law of Moses (
For God made human beings in his own image:
The death penalty has a theological basis. God’s image gives humans a unique status and authority within creation (
). Since murder destroys a person made in God’s image, the ultimate penalty must be imposed on a murderer. See also
. We are not to pursue personal revenge (
) but are to uphold the justice of the “governing authorities” that God has established (
Now be fruitful and multiply, and repopulate
(literally
swarm and fill
): In contrast to those who would destroy human life (
), God’s desire is that human life should abound and flourish.
God’s second post-flood speech conveys his promise and plan for preserving creation.
God had promised this
covenant
before the flood (

The story of Noah begins with him walking in righteousness and obeying the Lord (

), but it ends with him lying drunk and naked in his tent and then delivering a curse on Canaan. Even after the great flood, the human race exhibited some of the same sinful characteristics that warranted the judgment in the first place. Special attention is given to the cursed origin of the Canaanites, the corrupt and idolatrous people Israel would later displace from the Promised Land (see also
